issues.legal_issue: A public interest writ petition must provide a sufficient factual foundation even when strict pleading rules are relaxed.
material_facts: The petition sought urgent directions concerning displacement and rehabilitation but did not state how many people had vacated their homes or surrendered possession of their land.
The High Court obtained reports from the rehabilitation authority during the case, and those reports supplied facts on which further queries and proceedings were based.
issues.conclusion: The petition lacked the pleaded facts and supporting material needed for adjudication and should have been rejected at the threshold; the High Court erred in entertaining it on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: A party must plead and prove facts needed to substantiate a claim, and relief should not be granted on grounds outside the pleadings. In public interest litigation, technical pleading rules are applied flexibly, particularly where a layperson represents a disadvantaged group, but the petition must still provide a clear factual foundation and cannot seek a fishing or roving inquiry. The Court relied on Bharat Singh v. State of Haryana, Ram Sarup Gupta v. Bishun Narain Inter-College, Kalyan Singh Chouhan v. C.P. Joshi, Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendera v. State of U.P., A. Hamsaveni v. State of Tamil Nadu, Ashok Kumar Pandey v. State of West Bengal, and A. Abdul Farook v. Municipal Council, Perambalur.

predicates.public_interest_writ: A petitioner brings a writ proceeding on behalf of a group or for a claimed public cause.
predicates.lacks_material_factual_foundation: The petition omits material facts and supporting information needed to assess the claimed wrong and requested relief.

issues.definition: When a public interest writ lacks the factual foundation needed to assess the claim, it should not be entertained.

issues.legal_issue: An unexplained, belated challenge to a substantially completed development project should not be examined beyond issues concerning rehabilitation.
material_facts: Construction of the dam began years before the petition was filed and had been completed by then.
Large public investments had been made, and no objection had been raised at an earlier stage.
The petition gave no explanation for approaching the court so late, while also raising concerns about rehabilitation.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have examined issues other than the implementation of rehabilitation measures.
issues.legal_principle: A public interest litigant may not ordinarily challenge a development policy or project after substantial public expenditure and a lengthy unexplained delay. The Court relied on Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000), State of Maharashtra v. Digambar, and the distinction drawn in the earlier decision that rehabilitation concerns could still warrant judicial attention to protect affected people.

rule.if: public_interest_project_challenge and project_substantially_completed and substantial_public_investment and unexplained_delay

predicates.public_interest_project_challenge: A public interest proceeding challenges a development project or decisions associated with it.
predicates.project_substantially_completed: The project has been substantially constructed or completed before the proceeding is brought.
predicates.substantial_public_investment: A substantial amount of public money has already been spent on the project.
predicates.unexplained_delay: The petitioner gives no adequate explanation for waiting to bring the challenge.

issues.definition: When a public interest project challenge is brought after substantial completion and investment following an unexplained delay, only rehabilitation issues should remain for examination.

issues.legal_issue: Individual factual grievances about implementation of a rehabilitation scheme should ordinarily be raised first before the designated grievance authority.
material_facts: A grievance redressal authority had been established to consider rehabilitation grievances.
No oustee was shown to have approached that authority before the public interest petition was filed.
The disputes included individual factual questions about rehabilitation and entitlements.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should have directed the oustees to approach the grievance redressal authority first, with recourse to the High Court available to a person aggrieved by its decision.
issues.legal_principle: Where a designated grievance authority is established to adjudicate factual disputes concerning rehabilitation, those disputes should ordinarily be placed before it at first instance. A court may entertain a matter if an extraordinary situation arises. The Court relied on Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2005).

predicates.individual_rehabilitation_dispute: An affected person raises a factual dispute about that person's rehabilitation or resettlement entitlement.
predicates.designated_grievance_authority_available: A designated authority exists to hear and decide such rehabilitation grievances.

issues.definition: An individual rehabilitation dispute should ordinarily be taken first to the available authority established to decide it.

issues.legal_issue: A court should not decide the validity of a policy amendment when no relief to set it aside was sought and the issue was not brought before it on appeal.
material_facts: The amendment's validity was raised in a rejoinder, but the petitioner had not asked the High Court to quash it.
The High Court had not set the amendment aside, and the petitioner had not appealed on that issue.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to determine the validity of the amendment; it also set aside the High Court's comment on the State's competence to amend the policy.
issues.legal_principle: A court should not grant relief that a party has not sought. Where a plea has been raised but not properly considered, the appropriate course is to seek review; the Court relied on State of Maharashtra v. Ramdas Shrinivas Nayak, Transmission Corporation of A.P. Ltd. v. P. Surya Bhagavan, and Mount Carmel School Society v. DDA.

predicates.policy_amendment_challenge: A party disputes the validity of an amendment to a governing policy.
predicates.no_relief_to_set_aside_sought: The party has not asked the court to quash or set aside the amendment.
predicates.issue_not_brought_on_appeal: The party has not appealed the failure to decide the amendment's validity.

issues.definition: A court should not decide a policy amendment's validity when the party neither sought its invalidation nor brought that issue before the court on appeal.

issues.legal_issue: Lawful acquisition of property does not, by itself, violate the displaced owner's fundamental right to life, although the owner remains entitled to resettlement and rehabilitation under the applicable policy.
material_facts: Land was acquired for a public project, displacing people whose residence or livelihood was connected to it.
The displaced persons claimed that displacement without proper rehabilitation violated their right to life.
The project had a rehabilitation and resettlement policy applicable to its oustees.
issues.conclusion: Acquisition does not itself violate a constitutional or fundamental right of displaced persons, but they are entitled to resettlement and rehabilitation under the policy applicable to the project.
issues.legal_principle: The right to property under Article 300-A is a constitutional right, and deprivation of property under lawful acquisition does not, by itself, establish a violation of Article 21. Displaced persons are nevertheless entitled to rehabilitation under the applicable policy. The Court relied on Article 21 and Article 300-A of the Constitution, Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat, Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000), State of Kerala v. Peoples Union for Civil Liberties, Chameli Singh v. State of U.P., and Samatha v. State of A.P.

predicates.constitutional_claim_based_on_lawful_lan: A displaced person claims a constitutional violation on the basis that property was lawfully acquired for a project.
predicates.applicable_rehabilitation_policy: A rehabilitation policy applies to the people displaced by the project.

issues.definition: Lawful acquisition alone does not establish a fundamental-rights violation, but displaced persons remain entitled to rehabilitation under the applicable policy.

issues.legal_issue: Government policy choices are reviewable only on limited grounds, and the phrase ‘as far as possible’ confers discretion rather than an unconditional duty.
material_facts: The rehabilitation policy provided for agricultural land allotment ‘as far as possible’.
The State relied on resource constraints and the difficulty of obtaining land, while the record showed no attempt to acquire or purchase land for the oustees.
The policy amendment and its validity were not properly before the Court for a decision on the merits.
issues.conclusion: The phrase ‘as far as possible’ gives the authority discretion, not an absolute obligation; a court should not interfere with its exercise unless the decision is palpably arbitrary. Policy choices are not reviewable merely because another choice might seem preferable.
issues.legal_principle: Government may change policy in response to ground realities. A policy is ordinarily not subject to judicial review unless it conflicts with constitutional or statutory provisions or is arbitrary, irrational, or an abuse of power. ‘As far as possible’ denotes discretion, to be exercised in the particular circumstances, and not compulsion. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Ram Lubhaya Bagga, Ram Singh Vijay Pal Singh v. State of U.P., Villianur Iyarkkai Padukappu Maiyam v. Union of India, Iridium India Telecom Ltd. v. Motorola Inc., and High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan v. Veena Verma.

predicates.government_policy_decision: A government authority makes a decision while implementing or applying a public policy.
predicates.policy_uses_qualified_language: The policy qualifies the relevant direction in a way that allows for practical exceptions or discretion.

issues.definition: A qualified policy direction leaves room for discretion, and the resulting choice is reviewable only on limited grounds.

issues.legal_issue: A party is excused from performing a legal duty only when performance is impossible without fault and beyond that party's control.
material_facts: The State argued that obtaining land for oustees was impossible because cultivable land was scarce.
The record contained no evidence that the State had attempted to acquire or purchase land for their rehabilitation.
issues.conclusion: The State's claim of impossibility was unsubstantiated and did not excuse its failure to take steps toward rehabilitation.
issues.legal_principle: The maxims lex non cogit ad impossibilia and impossibilium nulla obligatio est excuse performance where a party, without fault and without control over the circumstances, is disabled from performing a duty. Impossibility does not remove a provision's mandatory character. The Court relied on Chandra Kishore Jha v. Mahavir Prasad, Hira Tikkoo v. Union Territory, Chandigarh, and Haryana Urban Development Authority v. Dr. Babeswar Kanhar.

predicates.party_claims_performance_impossible: A party says that it could not perform a legal duty.
predicates.no_fault_and_no_control: The inability arose without fault by the party and from circumstances beyond its control.
predicates.inability_is_substantiated: Evidence supports the claim that performance was genuinely impossible.

issues.definition: A party is excused for nonperformance only when genuine impossibility is established and arose without its fault or control.

issues.legal_issue: Eligible displaced landholders who have not voluntarily taken compensation or rehabilitation benefits in place of land may receive agricultural land as far as possible under the rehabilitation policy.
material_facts: The policy contemplated agricultural land allotment as far as possible and required an application from a displaced family seeking land rather than full compensation.

The State had deposited compensation into oustees' accounts, but the record did not establish that every oustee had voluntarily accepted compensation or a special rehabilitation grant in place of land.
The State had not attempted to acquire or purchase land for the oustees, and land suitability remained a matter for the grievance redressal authority.
The policy provided for assistance with the difference between compensation and land cost for specified categories if land could not be made available.
issues.conclusion: Displaced families who had not voluntarily withdrawn the special rehabilitation grant or compensation and who applied for land were entitled to agricultural land as far as possible under the policy. The State had to make government or private land available where possible, assist with purchase, and apply the policy's grant-in-aid provisions if land was unavailable.
issues.legal_principle: The applicable policy governs rehabilitation; its ‘as far as possible’ qualification allows practical discretion but does not permit authorities to dispense with their obligations without attempting to obtain land. Land for land is not an unconditional entitlement in every case, and relief must be assessed under the policy, including its provisions for assistance with land costs. The Court relied on the rehabilitation policy, Articles 37, 38, 39, 41, 43, 46 and 47 of the Constitution, Gramin Sewa Sanstha v. State of M.P., Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000), State of Kerala v. Peoples Union for Civil Liberties, and K. Krishna Reddy v. Special Deputy Collector.

predicates.project_displaced_landholder: A person who held land is displaced by a project and seeks rehabilitation.
predicates.has_not_voluntarily_taken_substitute_ben: The displaced person has not voluntarily accepted compensation or an additional rehabilitation benefit in place of seeking land.
predicates.applies_for_land: The displaced person applies to the responsible authority for agricultural land.

issues.definition: A displaced landholder who has not voluntarily taken substitute benefits and applies for land is entitled to allotment as far as possible under the applicable policy.

issues.legal_issue: A major son is not entitled to a separate allotment of agricultural land merely because the policy defines him as a separate family.
material_facts: The policy defined a son who had attained majority by the relevant notification date as a separate family.
The acquisition concerned the family's landholding, not a separately acquired holding belonging to each major son.
Treating each major son as separately entitled to a minimum allotment could give some families substantially more land than the area acquired and produce unequal or excessive benefits.
The earlier decisions concerning another project had proceeded on the mistaken assumption that a water-dispute award provided major sons that entitlement; the award did not do so.
issues.conclusion: Major sons are not entitled to separate agricultural-land allotments under this policy, although they may receive other benefits under it and may share in land allotted to the tenure holder according to applicable law.
issues.legal_principle: A policy definition must be read with its eligibility criteria and the scheme as a whole; it cannot be expanded to create an entitlement that the text and structure do not provide. Earlier decisions do not bind where they rest on a mistaken assumption about a controlling award or materially different circumstances. The Court relied on the policy definition of displaced family, the absence of such an entitlement in the water-dispute award, Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000 and 2005), Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Gurnam Kaur, State of Haryana v. Dharam Singh, State of West Bengal v. Kesoram Industries, Hotel Balaji v. State of A.P., and the principles of statutory interpretation discussed in Directorate of Enforcement v. Deepak Mahajan.

predicates.project_rehabilitation_claim: A person seeks agricultural land under a project's rehabilitation scheme.
predicates.claimant_is_major_son: The claimant is a son who had attained majority by the relevant eligibility date.
predicates.no_separate_landholding_acquired_for_cla: The acquired property was part of a family holding and no separate landholding belonging to the claimant was acquired.

issues.definition: A major son whose separate landholding was not acquired has no separate agricultural-land allotment entitlement merely by qualifying as a separate family.

issues.legal_issue: A landless displaced labourer is not entitled to agricultural land allotment where the applicable policy provides financial and livelihood assistance rather than an agricultural-land entitlement.
material_facts: The rehabilitation policy did not provide agricultural land allotment to landless labourers.
The project clearance referred to extending rehabilitation to landless labourers and affected people ‘as permissible’.
The policy and project plan provided landless families with financial support and assistance that could be used to acquire productive assets, including land.
Landless labourers had no acquired land for which acquisition compensation could be retained toward an allotment.
issues.conclusion: Landless labourers were not entitled to an allotment of agricultural land under the policy or clearance condition, but remained entitled to the specified financial and other rehabilitation benefits.
issues.legal_principle: A policy must be read as a whole; a party may not rely on an isolated word or phrase to create an entitlement inconsistent with the scheme. The words ‘as permissible’ limit the benefit to what the governing law or policy allows. The Court relied on the rehabilitation policy, the project plan, the clearance condition, Gurbax Singh v. State of Punjab, Municipal Committee, Patiala v. Model Town Residents Association, and Jagjit Cotton Textile Mills v. Chief Commercial Superintendent.

predicates.project_rehabilitation_claim: A person seeks agricultural land as rehabilitation following displacement by a project.
predicates.claimant_is_landless_labourer: The claimant was a landless labourer and did not hold agricultural land before displacement.
predicates.policy_provides_no_land_allotment: The applicable rehabilitation scheme provides no agricultural-land allotment for landless labourers.

issues.definition: A landless labourer has no agricultural-land allotment entitlement when the applicable scheme provides no such benefit.

issues.legal_issue: A water-dispute award made for a particular inter-state project does not govern rehabilitation for a separate project absent language extending it to that project.
material_facts: The award was made to resolve water disputes among several States and addressed rehabilitation for a different, identified dam project.
The award assigned costs and specified rehabilitation arrangements for the affected families of that project.
The award contained no provision applying its rehabilitation terms to future or separate projects.
The party seeking to apply the award to the project at issue identified no award term extending it to that project.
issues.conclusion: The award did not apply to the project at issue and could not supply an entitlement for its oustees.
issues.legal_principle: An award must be construed in the context of the dispute, project, and people it addresses; a provision concerning a particular project is not extended to a different project without language supporting that result. The Court relied on the award made under the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956, including its project-specific rehabilitation and implementation provisions.

predicates.rehabilitation_claim_for_separate_projec: Affected people seek rehabilitation benefits for a project different from the one addressed by an award.
predicates.award_is_project_specific: The award sets out rehabilitation arrangements for an identified project and its affected families.
predicates.no_extension_to_separate_project: The award contains no term extending its rehabilitation arrangements to the separate project.

issues.definition: A project-specific award does not govern rehabilitation for a separate project when it contains no extension to that project.

issues.legal_issue: Oustees of villages submerged under court orders may seek the same rehabilitation relief as other eligible oustees through individual adjudication.
material_facts: Five villages had been submerged while litigation was pending and following court orders.
There were conflicting accounts about whether the oustees had voluntarily accepted compensation or special rehabilitation grants.
The record was insufficient to determine each person's entitlement, and the grievance redressal authority could decide individual claims.
issues.conclusion: The oustees were entitled to the relief available to other eligible oustees; any person dissatisfied with the State's provision could approach the grievance redressal authority and establish an individual claim.
issues.legal_principle: A person should not suffer because of an act of the court, and people whose villages were submerged under court orders should not face hostile discrimination. Individual factual claims should be adjudicated by the designated grievance authority. The Court relied on the rehabilitation policy and the principle that no person should suffer from an act of the court.

predicates.oustees_submerged_under_court_orders: People's homes or land were submerged while the dispute was pending under court orders.
predicates.individual_entitlement_facts_unresolved: The record does not establish whether each person accepted substitute benefits or otherwise qualifies for relief.

issues.definition: When court-ordered submergence affects oustees whose individual entitlements remain unresolved, they may seek the same policy relief through individual adjudication.

issues.legal_issue: For compulsory acquisition, symbolic possession is sufficient for vacant and unoccupied land in appropriate circumstances, but actual physical possession is required for cultivated land or land with structures unless the authority already holds it or another recognized circumstance applies.
material_facts: The disputed land was agricultural and contained standing crops and numerous dwelling houses.
The original tenure holders remained in possession, continued cultivation, and had not been offered the promised rehabilitation land.
A court-appointed inspection confirmed that the tenure holders, rather than the acquiring authority, were in actual physical possession.
Revenue-record entries and mutation did not establish that possession had been taken.
issues.conclusion: Actual physical possession had not been taken, and the land had not vested in the State on that basis; the State could therefore withdraw the acquisition proceedings, subject to the separate ruling concerning submergence and the dwelling units.
issues.legal_principle: There is no universal formula for possession under Sections 16 and 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Symbolic possession may suffice for vacant, unoccupied land, while actual physical possession is required where crops or structures remain, unless the acquiring authority already possesses the land or a comparable circumstance applies. Revenue mutation does not create or establish title or possession. The Court relied on Sections 16, 17 and 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Balwant Narayan Bhagde v. M.D. Bhagwat, State of Tamil Nadu v. Mahalakshmi Ammal, Balmokand Khatri Educational and Industrial Trust v. State of Punjab, P.K. Kalburqui v. State of Karnataka, National Thermal Power Corporation v. Mahesh Datta, and Suman Verma v. Union of India.

predicates.compulsory_land_acquisition: A public authority seeks to acquire land compulsorily.
predicates.cultivated_or_built_land: The land contains crops or structures rather than being vacant and unoccupied.
predicates.landholders_remain_in_actual_possession: The former landholders continue to occupy or use the land and the authority has not taken actual physical possession.

issues.definition: Symbolic possession does not complete acquisition of cultivated or built land when the former landholders remain in actual possession.

issues.legal_issue: Agricultural land temporarily affected by brief backwater submergence need not be acquired, but dwelling units within the affected area remain subject to acquisition and rehabilitation requirements.
material_facts: Expert evidence established that the agricultural land lay between the full reservoir level and the backwater level and would be submerged only temporarily for fewer than fifteen days in an exceptional flood.
The expert evidence indicated that temporary flooding would benefit the soil through silting.
The affected area contained 167 dwelling units.
The State proposed to raise roads so that the area would not be left inaccessible.
issues.conclusion: The State could abandon acquisition of the agricultural land affected only by brief temporary submergence, but that conclusion did not apply to the 167 dwelling units, whose occupants were entitled to the applicable rehabilitation benefits.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Central Water Commission's 1997 guidelines for river-valley projects, acquisition of land between the full reservoir and maximum water levels depends on the duration and nature of submergence; the expert evidence supported non-acquisition of agricultural land subject to temporary submergence for fewer than fifteen days. Structures in the affected area should be acquired, and persons whose dwelling units are acquired are entitled to rehabilitation under the applicable policy. The Court also considered the project-specific terms of the water-dispute award and its earlier decision in Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2005).

predicates.dam_project: A public authority is carrying out a dam or river-valley project.
predicates.agricultural_land_only_temporarily_subme: The agricultural land lies within a temporary backwater-submergence area and is not permanently submerged.
predicates.submergence_under_fifteen_days: Expert evidence establishes that the temporary submergence lasts fewer than fifteen days.

issues.definition: For a dam project, brief temporary submergence does not require acquisition of the affected agricultural land, while affected dwelling units remain subject to acquisition and rehabilitation.

issues.legal_issue: An intentional material false statement made to mislead a court and obtain a favourable order may amount to criminal contempt, but the court may dispose of contempt applications without further order where doing so would serve no purpose.
material_facts: A public interest litigant asserted that landholders had been dispossessed, but a court-directed inspection found that they remained in possession and continued cultivating the land.
The Court found that submissions made for the litigant on possession were factually incorrect and unsupported.
Both sides filed applications seeking action under the contempt procedure.
The Court decided that dealing further with those applications would serve no purpose, while directing that future presentations by the litigant be scrutinized carefully.
issues.conclusion: The Court criticized the misleading conduct, stated that intentional false statements to obtain a favourable order may amount to criminal contempt, and disposed of the contempt applications without further order.
issues.legal_principle: A party seeking relief must make full and truthful disclosure of material facts. An intentional false statement made to mislead the court and obtain a favourable order may amount to criminal contempt because it obstructs the administration of justice. The Court relied on the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, Section 340, and Naraindas v. Government of Madhya Pradesh, Advocate General, State of Bihar v. Madhya Pradesh Khair Industries, Afzal v. State of Haryana, and K.D. Sharma v. Steel Authority of India.

predicates.contempt_application_in_public_interest_: A party asks the court to initiate or pursue contempt proceedings in a public interest matter.
predicates.material_statement_misleads_court: A party makes an objectively false statement about a material fact that misleads the court.
predicates.further_order_would_serve_no_purpose: The court concludes that further adjudication of the contempt application would serve no useful purpose.

issues.definition: A court may dispose of a contempt application without further order when a material statement misled it but further proceedings would serve no purpose.
